task_examples: Materials and fictional brief: Fictional note: “The desk is always confusing. A slip was hard to find on Monday, four slips were found quickly on Tuesday, and nobody recorded where the slips were placed.” The days and events are invented. Use this note and a blank sheet.

Scope and conditions: Use only your own non-sensitive materials or the supplied fiction. No paid tool, account, outside contact or public posting is required. A willing partner already present is optional except where live interaction is explicitly needed; solo preparation never counts as another person’s feedback. Stop or pause at any point. Timing is a flexible planning aid, not a performance limit.
Step 1: Underline observations, evaluative words and missing information using three labels rather than relying on colour. Do not upgrade “always confusing” into a measured fact.

Step 2: Write a narrower question that names an action and a condition: for example, what happens when the slips have one labelled place? List what “hard to find” would need to mean in an observation.
Step 3: Draw a small observation plan with the same item set and one layout change. State what you would record and what this small plan would not establish.
Step 4: Rewrite the question once after finding a missing condition. Keep both versions and one alternative question rather than forcing a single correct formulation.
Record and completion: Keep a known/unknown/assumption list, two versions of the question and a proposed observation. No experiment or fictional observation becomes a measured personal result.

Reflection: Which part made you curious: defining words, isolating a condition or designing an observation? Would you want to investigate the revised question? Note if the topic itself was uninteresting.
Boundaries: No new user study, timings, participant claims or data collection is required. A question plan is the output; do not invent results to finish it.

Optional continuation: Optional: take one additional short round of this same exercise, changing one condition named in your reflection. Keep the two records; do not treat ease or improvement as an interest score. Optional, up to two hours only if useful: develop this same small output with materials already available. Use only fictional or your own non-sensitive material; no outside contact or spending. Stop after a documented revision rather than filling the time. Optional: repeat this same exercise twice on dates you choose, changing one condition and noting engagement and effort. These observations do not establish a lasting interest or validate a test.

task_examples: Materials and fictional brief: Three invented source cards concern a paper holder. Card A, an observation note: “With ten cards, the base moved during one removal; pull direction not recorded.” Card B, a material note: “This model used thin paper; no comparison with thick card.” Card C, a comment: “I like the appearance; I did not try removing a card.” None is an external research source.

Scope and conditions: Use only your own non-sensitive materials or the supplied fiction. No paid tool, account, outside contact or public posting is required. A willing partner already present is optional except where live interaction is explicitly needed; solo preparation never counts as another person’s feedback. Stop or pause at any point. Timing is a flexible planning aid, not a performance limit.
Step 1: Write a question: what do these notes tell us about using the holder? Keep the three source labels and their exact stated limitations.
Step 2: For each card, record the claim it supports and one claim it cannot support. Appearance approval cannot establish ease of removal; a single movement cannot explain its cause.
Step 3: Place one apparent disagreement side by side. Decide whether it is a real contradiction or concerns different aspects. Mark missing corroboration instead of counting notes as votes.
Step 4: Write a cautious two-sentence account and the next evidence you would want. Do not search for people, buy materials or claim that the invented cards establish real product facts.
Record and completion: Produce a three-row evidence table: source card, observation or opinion, supported statement, limit and next evidence. Retain “unknown” when no card answers the question.
Reflection: Did comparing scope and uncertainty make you want to examine another source? Did you prefer resolving the question quickly? Keep that response separate from the quality of your summary.
Boundaries: All three cards are fictional teaching material. They are not three genuine independent sources, peer-reviewed findings or evidence of an occupation.

task_examples: Materials and fictional brief: Fictional log: “A paper holder moved in one trial with ten cards and stayed still in another with five. Pull direction and base arrangement were not controlled.” This is invented, not an experimental finding.

Scope and conditions: Use only your own non-sensitive materials or the supplied fiction. No paid tool, account, outside contact or public posting is required. A willing partner already present is optional except where live interaction is explicitly needed; solo preparation never counts as another person’s feedback. Stop or pause at any point. Timing is a flexible planning aid, not a performance limit.
Step 1: Write two possible explanations that could account for the note. For each, name an observation that would be consistent with it and one that would make you question it.
Step 2: Design one safe comparison using only paper materials: keep one proposed condition fixed and change one other. State which details remain uncontrolled.

Step 3: Write predicted observations as “if this explanation is useful, I might see…” without filling in a result. Running the comparison is optional; any real observation must be separately labelled.
Step 4: Review whether both explanations still could hold. Keep an unresolved alternative and a next check; do not treat a single small comparison as proof.
Record and completion: Keep a hypothesis table with explanation, prediction, challenging observation, planned control, actual observation or unperformed, and revised uncertainty.
Reflection: Which part held your attention: proposing explanations, looking for counterexamples or revising a plan? Would you repeat the reasoning with a familiar, less attractive topic?
Boundaries: No score, statistical significance, causal proof or ability inference. Do not fabricate observations or extend this paper task into machinery or risky experiments.

task_examples: Materials and fictional brief: Invented neutral scene: “A small room has one table, an open window and a sealed envelope.” The envelope has no real owner or personal information. Use paper or a text editor.

Scope and conditions: Use only your own non-sensitive materials or the supplied fiction. No paid tool, account, outside contact or public posting is required. A willing partner already present is optional except where live interaction is explicitly needed; solo preparation never counts as another person’s feedback. Stop or pause at any point. Timing is a flexible planning aid, not a performance limit.
Step 1: Write a short description that makes the room feel welcoming, using only the supplied objects and clearly invented sensory details.
Step 2: Write a second description that makes the same room feel uncertain, then a third that makes it feel ordinary. Keep object facts consistent; frame invented details as part of fiction.
Step 3: Choose a phrase from each version and describe how its wording changes attention or atmosphere. There is no objectively best mood or audience reaction.
Step 4: Revise one version by changing its viewpoint or rhythm. Retain the first version and explain one deliberate choice and one part you would still explore.
Record and completion: Keep three short versions and one revision note. Completion is a set of expressive choices, not praise, a word-count target or a personality label.
Reflection: Did you want to find another phrase, viewpoint or emotional effect? Was revision satisfying or tiring? Could the same interest persist with a less appealing subject?
Boundaries: No real person’s story, diagnosis or stereotype. If you ask a willing person already present for a reaction, label it one person’s response; no outreach or publication is required.

task_examples: Materials and fictional brief: Fictional instructions: “Choose one paper kit. Write the kit name and planned return day. Place it in the return tray after use. If the tray is full, put a note beside it and leave the kit in its usual place.” No real service or policy is represented.

Scope and conditions: Use only your own non-sensitive materials or the supplied fiction. No paid tool, account, outside contact or public posting is required. A willing partner already present is optional except where live interaction is explicitly needed; solo preparation never counts as another person’s feedback. Stop or pause at any point. Timing is a flexible planning aid, not a performance limit.
Step 1: Sketch the four actions using words, arrows or simple shapes. Include the full-tray exception rather than hiding it in decoration.
Step 2: Make a second layout with a different reading order or grouping. Label every symbol in words so that colour alone carries no instruction.
Step 3: Follow each diagram yourself from start to finish, including the exception. Record a point where your own interpretation could be ambiguous; self-checking is not external usability evidence.
Step 4: Revise one label or arrangement. Keep both layouts and explain the change. A rough diagram with an explicit unresolved question can complete the exercise.

Record and completion: Keep two diagrams, the exception path and a revision note. Record any feedback only if a willing person already present actually supplies it; otherwise mark external feedback absent.
Reflection: Were you drawn to spacing, symbols, sequence or making the message easier to grasp? Would you want to revise again after a concrete misunderstanding?
Boundaries: This is an invented instructional diagram, not a real organisation’s procedure or an accessibility certification. No graphic-design aptitude or career conclusion follows.

task_examples: Materials and fictional brief: Fictional prompt: “An empty chair remains beside a table after a small gathering. A blue ribbon lies on the seat. Someone returns to the room.” Invent the people and their reasons; use no identifiable real experience.

Scope and conditions: Use only your own non-sensitive materials or the supplied fiction. No paid tool, account, outside contact or public posting is required. A willing partner already present is optional except where live interaction is explicitly needed; solo preparation never counts as another person’s feedback. Stop or pause at any point. Timing is a flexible planning aid, not a performance limit.
Step 1: Write a five-sentence scene with an opening action, a concrete detail, a change, a response and an ending. These are prompts, not a marking rubric.
Step 2: Underline one detail that shapes how you imagine the scene. Write a different opening or ending while keeping the ribbon and chair in the scene.
Step 3: Read both versions silently or aloud. Describe the change in emphasis in your own words; do not claim that every reader would feel the same emotion.
Step 4: Choose a detail to retain and a question you would explore in a longer scene. Stop with two versions and a brief note even if neither feels polished.
Record and completion: Keep the two versions and a note on viewpoint, atmosphere and the next revision you would choose. No ratings, public posting or third-party critique is required.
Reflection: Did imagining, selecting words or reshaping the scene make you want to continue? Separate embarrassment about rough writing from interest in the process.
Boundaries: No copyrighted story imitation, real-person disclosure or therapeutic interpretation. This is original fiction practice, not a writing ability or personality assessment.

task_examples: Materials and fictional brief: Fictional brief: a shared desk needs a place to keep five blank paper slips without blocking a reader’s notebook. Use five scraps of paper, one sheet as a pretend notebook and your own safe desk surface; no actual shared desk or user is being investigated.

Scope and conditions: Use only your own non-sensitive materials or the supplied fiction. No paid tool, account, outside contact or public posting is required. A willing partner already present is optional except where live interaction is explicitly needed; solo preparation never counts as another person’s feedback. Stop or pause at any point. Timing is a flexible planning aid, not a performance limit.
Step 1: Arrange the notebook sheet and five slips as a starting layout. Sketch it, including the edges of your working area. Write what the fictional user needs and what is still unspecified.

Step 2: Move one slip away and put it back three times. Observe paper movement, reach and obstruction. Record only what happens in your own setup; if you cannot try it, mark that observation unperformed.
Step 3: Change just the slip location and repeat the same action. Note which visible detail changed. Do not claim that a person elsewhere would find it easier.
Step 4: Keep the two sketches and one unresolved question. Choose a next observation, such as a different paper size, without buying materials or recruiting participants.

task_examples: Materials and fictional brief: Fictional observation card: “A paper holder moved when a card was removed. The desk surface and pulling direction were not recorded.” Reuse your IAR paper model if available, or fold a single scrap of paper into a holder for three blank slips. The observation card is invented, not a report of your trial.

Scope and conditions: Use only your own non-sensitive materials or the supplied fiction. No paid tool, account, outside contact or public posting is required. A willing partner already present is optional except where live interaction is explicitly needed; solo preparation never counts as another person’s feedback. Stop or pause at any point. Timing is a flexible planning aid, not a performance limit.
Step 1: Copy the fictional observation separately from anything you actually observe. List two possible explanations, such as how the holder rests or the direction of the pull; label them guesses.
Step 2: If you have a safe paper setup, repeat one removal and describe it without explaining the cause. Otherwise sketch the proposed observation and mark it unperformed.
Step 3: Change only one arrangement detail and repeat. A change that coincides with different movement does not settle the cause; record other uncontrolled details.
Step 4: Write one next check and one stopping condition. Stop after one comparison or when the setup cannot be tried safely; an unresolved cause is an acceptable completion.

Record and completion: Make columns for initial condition, observed action, possible explanation, single change, observed result and unresolved factors. Keep fictional and actual entries explicitly separated.
Reflection: Did you want to keep tracing the cause, or only finish fixing the object? Which uncertainty was interesting and which was frustrating? What condition would you change before another try?
Boundaries: Paper only: no dismantling devices, batteries, mains power, heat or moving mechanisms. This is not fault-finding certification or proof of technical ability.

content.title: Investigative
content.core_drive: Interest in asking questions, gathering evidence, and analyzing causes to understand why things work as they do. Reading research material, comparing explanations, and testing hypotheses are typical activities.
possible_drains: Research tasks often involve incomplete information, repeated checking, and accepting that conclusions remain uncertain. Different fields also require relevant knowledge and methodological training. Interest can be a starting point for learning.
context_costs: Research tasks often involve incomplete information, repeated checking, and accepting that conclusions remain uncertain. Different fields also require relevant knowledge and methodological training. Interest can be a starting point for learning.
misread_guardrails: Interest in research is distinct from intelligence, subject knowledge, and research skills. The score cannot demonstrate these abilities or determine a specific field of study.
validation_questions: Do I want to spend time checking evidence, modeling, and comparing evidence, or do I mainly want a quick answer?
What training, data access, or professional background does this question require?
When there is no clear answer, do I want to keep asking questions or move on to carrying something out?
content.positive_value: The appeal may lie in the question itself or in the process of checking evidence and reasoning. Notice whether you want to investigate inconsistencies, revise explanations, and keep exploring when there is no conclusion yet.
content.real_world_cost: Research tasks often involve incomplete information, repeated checking, and accepting that conclusions remain uncertain. Different fields also require relevant knowledge and methodological training. Interest can be a starting point for learning.
content.high_score_reading: In this response, you expressed greater interest in analysis and inquiry. You could first try looking up information, comparing evidence, or explaining a phenomenon, and observe which questions you want to explore in depth.
work_activity_examples: Turn a vague question into one that can be checked against evidence
Compare information from different sources
Propose different explanations for the same phenomenon
Design observations that distinguish between explanations
content.common_misread: Interest in research is distinct from intelligence, subject knowledge, and research skills. The score cannot demonstrate these abilities or determine a specific field of study.
content.action_advice: Choose a question you are curious about. Start with a question, evidence-checking, or hypothesis activity below, then look back at the step that most interested you.

boundaries.user_visible_boundary: The interpretations below describe interest in activities. Skills, qualifications, and career choices require other information as well.

content.title: Artistic
content.core_drive: Interest in creating, expressing ideas, and exploring different forms by turning ideas into writing, images, sound, or performance. These activities usually allow multiple forms of expression rather than one standard answer.
possible_drains: Creative work often involves revisions, feedback, deadlines, and audience requirements. Personal and commercial projects may offer different levels of freedom. Understanding these conditions can help you consider whether your interest will continue.
context_costs: Creative work often involves revisions, feedback, deadlines, and audience requirements. Personal and commercial projects may offer different levels of freedom. Understanding these conditions can help you consider whether your interest will continue.
misread_guardrails: The Artistic score reflects interest in creative activities. It does not evaluate the quality of your work, your creativity, or your aesthetic ability.
validation_questions: Which part do I most want to continue: developing ideas, choosing a style, refining versions, or adjusting after feedback?
What training, tools, aesthetic standards, or conditions for collaboration does this task require?
When the work is evaluated, does my interest grow, weaken, or shift to another part of the activity?
content.positive_value: The appeal may lie in developing a new angle, choosing a style, or repeatedly refining a piece of work. Distinguish whether you prefer creating freely, communicating to an audience, or improving existing content.
content.real_world_cost: Creative work often involves revisions, feedback, deadlines, and audience requirements. Personal and commercial projects may offer different levels of freedom. Understanding these conditions can help you consider whether your interest will continue.
content.high_score_reading: In this response, you expressed greater interest in creating and expressing ideas. You could first try different media, such as writing, visuals, or sound, and compare which forms you want to keep refining.
work_activity_examples: Develop different ways to express the same topic
Turn complex information into an explanatory diagram
Write, take photographs, or make a sound piece
Revise the structure and style of a piece of work in response to feedback
content.common_misread: The Artistic score reflects interest in creative activities. It does not evaluate the quality of your work, your creativity, or your aesthetic ability.
content.action_advice: Choose a form of expression below and finish a small piece of work. Then look back at whether you want to revise it and what you would change.

boundaries.user_visible_boundary: The interpretations below describe interest in activities. Skills, qualifications, and career choices require other information as well.

content.title: Realistic
content.core_drive: Interest in using tools, working with materials, or caring for tangible things through hands-on work with visible results. Repair, making things, operating equipment, and outdoor work can all involve these activities.
interest_activity_focus: Using tools and making physical objects
possible_drains: Physical demands, safety training, and coordination on site vary widely between settings. Enjoying model making does not necessarily mean enjoying long periods of outdoor work. Learning about specific tasks and conditions is more useful than looking only at job titles.
context_costs: Physical demands, safety training, and coordination on site vary widely between settings. Enjoying model making does not necessarily mean enjoying long periods of outdoor work. Learning about specific tasks and conditions is more useful than looking only at job titles.
misread_guardrails: Realistic interest does not mean strong practical skills, and it does not mean being limited to physical work. Actual skills and training conditions need separate consideration.
validation_questions: Which part do I most want to continue: working with tools and materials, troubleshooting on site, or turning steps into a visible result?
What training, safety requirements, or resources does this activity involve?
Does the interest remain when the setting or position of responsibility changes?
content.positive_value: The appeal of these activities often comes from working directly with something: adjusting a part, testing a material, or getting equipment running again. Notice whether you enjoy making things, troubleshooting, or seeing a tangible result.
content.real_world_cost: Physical demands, safety training, and coordination on site vary widely between settings. Enjoying model making does not necessarily mean enjoying long periods of outdoor work. Learning about specific tasks and conditions is more useful than looking only at job titles.
content.high_score_reading: In this response, you expressed greater interest in working hands-on with tangible things. You could first explore activities involving operating, making, or troubleshooting on site, then compare how different materials, tools, and work settings feel to you.
work_activity_examples: Assemble or repair a simple object
Make and adjust a physical model
Observe equipment in operation and record anything unusual
Compare how materials differ in practical use
content.common_misread: Realistic interest does not mean strong practical skills, and it does not mean being limited to physical work. Actual skills and training conditions need separate consideration.
content.action_advice: Choose something familiar from the activities below and try operating it or observing it. Afterwards, look back at the part you most wanted to continue.

content.title: Social
content.core_drive: Interest in helping people understand problems, learn, and grow through explaining, listening, guiding, or supporting. The focus is on the process of helping people, rather than simply how often you interact with them.
possible_drains: Supporting others requires communication, patience, and clear limits of responsibility. Some roles also involve professional qualifications and emotional demands. Everyday help and professional services have different requirements.
context_costs: Supporting others requires communication, patience, and clear limits of responsibility. Some roles also involve professional qualifications and emotional demands. Everyday help and professional services have different requirements.
misread_guardrails: Social interest does not mean being outgoing, kind, or well liked. An interest in helping others also cannot replace the professional training needed for teaching, counseling, or care.
validation_questions: Which part do I most want to continue: understanding needs, explaining information, offering companionship and support, or coordinating resources?
What ethical boundaries, professional training, or capacity to handle emotional demands does this interaction require?
Does my interest remain steady when responsibility increases or the person receiving support changes?
content.positive_value: The appeal may lie in understanding someone's needs, helping them learn something, or helping resolve a specific difficulty. Observe whether you prefer teaching, listening, or finding a way forward together.
content.real_world_cost: Supporting others requires communication, patience, and clear limits of responsibility. Some roles also involve professional qualifications and emotional demands. Everyday help and professional services have different requirements.
content.medium_score_reading: You may be willing to help others with familiar topics or within familiar relationships without wanting an ongoing support role. The person, communication style, and scope of responsibility may affect your willingness.
work_activity_examples: Explain a concept and respond to questions
Listen and check what the person actually needs
Help someone practice a skill you know
Organize materials suited to a particular learner
content.common_misread: Social interest does not mean being outgoing, kind, or well liked. An interest in helping others also cannot replace the professional training needed for teaching, counseling, or care.
content.action_advice: Choose a situation where you can offer everyday help within your abilities. With the other person's willingness to participate, look back at which kind of support you enjoyed.

content.title: Enterprising
content.core_drive: Interest in advancing goals, gaining support, coordinating resources, or influencing decisions. Starting projects, explaining proposals, negotiating, and organizing progress can all involve these activities.
possible_drains: Moving work forward often involves disagreement, pressure for results, and uncertainty. Decision-making authority, resources, and responsibility differ between roles. Enjoying starting projects does not mean wanting every management responsibility.
context_costs: Moving work forward often involves disagreement, pressure for results, and uncertainty. Decision-making authority, resources, and responsibility differ between roles. Enjoying starting projects does not mean wanting every management responsibility.
misread_guardrails: Enterprising interest does not mean you must start a business, and it does not demonstrate leadership or business judgment. It describes interest in influencing, organizing, and moving things forward.
validation_questions: Which part do I most want to continue: setting goals, securing resources, persuading people to collaborate, or making choices about risk?
What authority, resources, responsibility, and capacity to handle risk does this task require?
Am I still willing to keep moving it forward when the outcome is uncertain or feedback slows down?
content.positive_value: The appeal may lie in finding opportunities, persuading others, or moving something forward. Distinguish whether you prefer proposing a direction, securing resources, or coordinating implementation.
content.real_world_cost: Moving work forward often involves disagreement, pressure for results, and uncertainty. Decision-making authority, resources, and responsibility differ between roles. Enjoying starting projects does not mean wanting every management responsibility.
content.medium_score_reading: Your willingness to move things forward may depend on whether you support the goal and whether resources are available. Think back to where you wanted to take the initiative and where you preferred to help carry things out.
work_activity_examples: Explain a proposal to others and seek support
Compare the resources needed to reach a goal
Coordinate a group's responsibilities and progress
Discuss workable arrangements when views differ
content.common_misread: Enterprising interest does not mean you must start a business, and it does not demonstrate leadership or business judgment. It describes interest in influencing, organizing, and moving things forward.
content.action_advice: Choose a small shared task with clear responsibilities. Look back at whether you preferred initiating it, communicating, or organizing its execution.

content.title: Conventional
content.core_drive: Interest in organizing information, checking details, and maintaining processes under clear rules. Classifying, recording, checking data, and handling tasks in an orderly way are common activities.
possible_drains: Jobs differ in their demands for repetition, accuracy, and meeting deadlines. Enjoying organizing information does not necessarily mean enjoying long periods of repeated data entry. The clarity of a process and the reasonableness of its standards also affect the experience.
context_costs: Jobs differ in their demands for repetition, accuracy, and meeting deadlines. Enjoying organizing information does not necessarily mean enjoying long periods of repeated data entry. The clarity of a process and the reasonableness of its standards also affect the experience.
misread_guardrails: Conventional interest does not mean being conservative, lacking creativity, or being reliable at work. An interest score cannot replace an evaluation of attention to detail or actual work quality.
validation_questions: Which part do I most want to continue: organizing, checking, building a process, or keeping records consistent?
What understanding of rules, system access, or responsibility for errors does this task require?
Does my interest grow or decline when rules change or repetition increases?
content.positive_value: The appeal may lie in making information clear, finding errors, or keeping a process running steadily. Distinguish whether you prefer establishing order, following existing steps, or improving details.
content.real_world_cost: Jobs differ in their demands for repetition, accuracy, and meeting deadlines. Enjoying organizing information does not necessarily mean enjoying long periods of repeated data entry. The clarity of a process and the reasonableness of its standards also affect the experience.
content.low_score_safe_reading: In this response, activities with clear rules and substantial repetition held relatively limited appeal. This does not mean you are careless or unable to complete work according to standards.
work_activity_examples: Organize information and establish classification rules
Check the differences between two records
Write a procedure for a common task
Maintain a checklist and track the status of items
content.common_misread: Conventional interest does not mean being conservative, lacking creativity, or being reliable at work. An interest score cannot replace an evaluation of attention to detail or actual work quality.
content.action_advice: Choose a set of real information that contains nothing sensitive. Try organizing or checking it, then look back at whether you enjoyed the order, finding errors, or improving the process.

content.positive_value: The value of this content is to break the clues into observable small tasks: Investigative focuses on questions, evidence, mechanisms, variables, and ways of explaining; Artistic focuses on expression, style, narrative, form, and experience; Realistic focuses on tangible objects, tools, on-site conditions, materials, and visible results. Whichever comes first only indicates which activity to gather evidence from first. These clues offer exploration questions, not job answers.
content.real_world_cost: Reading boundary: these three clues may occur in different parts of one task or across different environments. Record only the appeal of specific activities, points of hesitation, and conditions you want to adjust. Do not turn the score order into a ranking of abilities or a fixed way of working.
content.activity_chain: Observe in order: first analyze questions, evidence, variables, or ways of explaining; then try different approaches to expression, style, narrative, or form; finally work with tangible objects, tools, or on-site conditions.
content.core_reading: These three leading interest dimensions indicate that Investigative, Artistic, Realistic activities stand relatively high in this response. IAR only sets a reading order: Investigative is the initial observation entry point, with Artistic and Realistic as additional entry points. It cannot establish a personality identity, ability level, or career conclusion.
content.first_experiment: Spend 30 minutes on a low-risk observation: first include an activity involving inquiry, then one involving expression, and finally one involving hands-on. Record only which part you most want to continue.
content.ordered_code_handling: IAR is the ordered three-letter code for this assessment: the first dimension, Investigative, is the initial observation entry point; the second, Artistic, and the third, Realistic, are additional entry points. The order changes what to ask first and what to explore next. It is not a fixed identity, an ability conclusion, or a career answer.
content.low_risk_validation: Low-risk observation: choose a small task that accommodates inquiry, expression, and hands-on clues. Record the three activities separately and look only at activity preferences and evidence of wanting to continue.
content.primary_activity_chain: Start with the first dimension, Investigative: use it as the initial observation entry point and look for small-task evidence involving questions, evidence, mechanisms, variables, and ways of explaining.
content.secondary_support_line: Then consider the second dimension, Artistic: use it as an additional observation entry point and record whether expression, style, narrative, form, and experience make the task more appealing.
content.tertiary_stabilizer: The third dimension, Realistic, is only an additional clue: observe whether tangible objects, tools, on-site conditions, materials, and visible results help distinguish more specific task conditions.
content.likely_tension: Differences between the three clues are worth exploring through small tasks. Observing one action and one condition at a time is more reliable than treating the three leading interests as a fixed way of working.
activity_sequence: Initial observation entry point: analyze questions, evidence, variables, or ways of explaining
Second observation entry point: try different approaches to expression, style, narrative, or form
Third observation entry point: work with tangible objects, tools, or on-site conditions
content.when_to_use_140q: When a user wants to distinguish whether task activities, environmental conditions, or role responsibilities are more appealing, 140Q can be an option. It only adds contextual detail; it does not increase accuracy or override 60Q.
content.when_not_to_overread: When response quality is low, the leading scores are close, content is missing, or the user only wants to see the names, return to observing activities rather than offering strong interpretations.
content.free_page_teaser: The Investigative, Artistic, Realistic interest clues can be observed in the order IAR without rushing to a career answer.
content.deep_report_extension: Further reading can distinguish preference evidence across tasks, environments, and role responsibilities, and offer exploration questions and follow-up actions.

boundaries.user_visible_boundary: This interpretation concerns the three leading activity-interest clues. It is not a personality type, a career conclusion, or a prediction of success.

context_costs: The tools, information, objects, or access needed for inquiry activities may be insufficient.
The time, feedback, collaboration, or standards needed for expression activities may differ.
Putting the two activities in the same situation may change the order of responsibilities and the evaluation criteria, which may affect your interest response.
validation_questions: Are these two activities consecutive steps, parallel responsibilities, or competing for time?
Which activity is more affected by the environment, resources, training, or pace of feedback?
If only one activity remains, does your interest become clearer or weaker?
content.pair_tension: Tension in the combination often appears when a task rewards only one of the activities: inquiry clues may involve breaking down a question, checking evidence, comparing variables, or setting out an explanation, while expression clues may involve drafting an expression, adjusting style, rewriting a narrative, or making versions in different forms. A specific situation is needed to check whether these are consecutive steps, parallel responsibilities, or activities that drain each other.
content.micro_experiment: Spend 30 minutes on a two-column observation: record inquiry activities on the left and expression activities on the right. Compare only activity preferences, the demands of the conditions, and next questions; do not draw a career conclusion.

faq_items.q: How do I read a three-letter code? For example, IAS?
faq_items.a: In the example IAS, I means Investigative, A means Artistic, and S means Social. Read the three letters shown in your own report as the interest dimensions that stand out in that result. Their order describes that result ranking, not a fixed identity.

faq_items.q: Does this tell me which career I should choose?
faq_items.a: No. It points to work activities that may be worth exploring or validating first. Real choices also depend on ability, experience, opportunity, values, entry barriers, and market conditions.

faq_items.q: Does a score of 80 mean I scored higher than 80% of people?
faq_items.a: No. The current 0-100 score is a within-form interest-strength conversion. It is not a population percentile and it is not an ability score.

faq_items.q: Does low E mean I cannot start a business, sell, or manage?
faq_items.a: No. Low E only means high-persuasion, high-exposure, and high-competition activities may not be the most natural interest entry point. Capability still depends on skills, experience, and real opportunities.

faq_items.q: Does low R mean I cannot do technical or hands-on work?
faq_items.a: No. Low R does not mean clumsy or unable to learn technical work. It means tools, field work, and physical operation may not be the most natural interest entry point right now.

faq_items.q: Is 140Q more accurate?
faq_items.a: Do not read it that way. 140Q observes tasks, environments, and role responsibilities in more context. It does not overturn 60Q and it does not compare raw scores across forms.

faq_items.q: What if I disagree with the result?
faq_items.a: Record the disagreement, check answer quality, near ties, and activity imagination, then use low-risk experiments or a same-form retest to validate. Feedback does not change scores.

faq_items.q: Why are occupation examples not expanded into a direct list?
faq_items.a: Occupation names are easy to misread as conclusions. FermatMind shows activities and tasks first. Occupation names are only context examples and must keep source status visible.

faq_items.q: Can I share the report with a teacher, counselor, or friend?
faq_items.a: Start with the safe share version. When a full report includes personal interest structure or feedback history, you should decide whether to show it.

faq_items.q: Can an employer use this for screening?
faq_items.a: No. This report must not be used for recruiting, admission, promotion, elimination, or qualification decisions.

faq_items.q: Why does the result page include Action Lab?
faq_items.a: Career interests need real-world validation. Action Lab supports low-risk experiments and does not generate career conclusions.

faq_items.q: What if a retest looks different?
faq_items.a: First check whether it used the same form, answer quality, near ties, and your state at the time. Do not chart raw score gains or drops across different forms.

faq_items.q: Can a Holland Code change over time?
faq_items.a: Interest structure often has some stability, but experience, opportunity, and environment can affect expression. Treat retesting as a clue about change, not a win-or-lose result.

faq_items.q: How is this different from an ability test?
faq_items.a: RIASEC looks at interest in activities. It does not decide whether you are already good at them. Ability needs other evidence.

faq_items.q: Why not just tell me the single path I should take?
faq_items.a: A direct conclusion can hide real-world constraints. A steadier approach is to read activities, tasks, environments, and roles first, then test small next steps.

faq_items.q: If I already have a target occupation, should I still read RIASEC?
faq_items.a: Yes. Put the target into aspiration calibration and read which activities overlap with current interest clues, and which real-world parts still need validation.

faq_items.q: Can I show the PDF to a counselor?
faq_items.a: Yes, but once a PDF is forwarded the platform cannot remotely recall it. A counselor discussion version should be used only with your permission.

faq_items.q: Why does the result page not show every score detail by default?
faq_items.a: The default view shows levels and explanations to reduce false precision. Expanded views can show more evidence when appropriate.

faq_items.q: Is a higher score always better?
faq_items.a: No. High interest can be a more natural energy entry point, but it can also carry practical costs. Low interest is not a defect.

faq_items.q: Can I use this report to choose a college major?
faq_items.a: It can be an exploration input, but not the only basis. Major decisions also depend on course content, ability foundation, portfolio, resources, location, and long-term commitment.

activities.activity_label: Turn a broad question into an observable question
activities.activity_user_copy: Original English teaching exercise, written 24 October 2026; all supplied situations, notes and quantities are fictional. No new user study, timings, participant claims or data collection is required. A question plan is the output; do not invent results to finish it. The single-letter family below is inherited from the existing FermatMind editorial identity, not newly assigned or validated here. Observe willingness to repeat and contextual effort; do not score performance, infer skills or job fit, or change measured scores, Top3 or snapshots. Keep other interests open when scores are close or broad. This package does not provide EN16 six-dimension interpretation.
activities.source_name: FermatTest RIASEC Activity Task Examples v1
task_examples: Materials and fictional brief: Fictional note: “The desk is always confusing. A slip was hard to find on Monday, four slips were found quickly on Tuesday, and nobody recorded where the slips were placed.” The days and events are invented. Use this note and a blank sheet.

Scope and conditions: Use only your own non-sensitive materials or the supplied fiction. No paid tool, account, outside contact or public posting is required. A willing partner already present is optional except where live interaction is explicitly needed; solo preparation never counts as another person’s feedback. Stop or pause at any point. Timing is a flexible planning aid, not a performance limit.
Step 1: Underline observations, evaluative words and missing information using three labels rather than relying on colour. Do not upgrade “always confusing” into a measured fact.

Step 2: Write a narrower question that names an action and a condition: for example, what happens when the slips have one labelled place? List what “hard to find” would need to mean in an observation.
Step 3: Draw a small observation plan with the same item set and one layout change. State what you would record and what this small plan would not establish.
Step 4: Rewrite the question once after finding a missing condition. Keep both versions and one alternative question rather than forcing a single correct formulation.
Record and completion: Keep a known/unknown/assumption list, two versions of the question and a proposed observation. No experiment or fictional observation becomes a measured personal result.

Reflection: Which part made you curious: defining words, isolating a condition or designing an observation? Would you want to investigate the revised question? Note if the topic itself was uninteresting.
Boundaries: No new user study, timings, participant claims or data collection is required. A question plan is the output; do not invent results to finish it.

Optional continuation: Optional: take one additional short round of this same exercise, changing one condition named in your reflection. Keep the two records; do not treat ease or improvement as an interest score. Optional, up to two hours only if useful: develop this same small output with materials already available. Use only fictional or your own non-sensitive material; no outside contact or spending. Stop after a documented revision rather than filling the time. Optional: repeat this same exercise twice on dates you choose, changing one condition and noting engagement and effort. These observations do not establish a lasting interest or validate a test.

Origin: Original English teaching exercise, written 24 October 2026; all supplied situations, notes and quantities are fictional. Conceptual sources are U.S. O*NET public descriptions checked 24 October 2026; publication year unknown. No O*NET item, occupational record or formal activity code is imported. Domain and independent review have not occurred.

Reflection: Record separately whether you wanted to investigate, generate alternatives or continue making adjustments. Rough work may reflect practice; polished work does not establish a wish to continue.

task_examples: Materials and fictional brief: Fictional observation card: “A paper holder moved when a card was removed. The desk surface and pulling direction were not recorded.” Reuse your IAR paper model if available, or fold a single scrap of paper into a holder for three blank slips. The observation card is invented, not a report of your trial.

Scope and conditions: Use only your own non-sensitive materials or the supplied fiction. No paid tool, account, outside contact or public posting is required. A willing partner already present is optional except where live interaction is explicitly needed; solo preparation never counts as another person’s feedback. Stop or pause at any point. Timing is a flexible planning aid, not a performance limit.
Step 1: Copy the fictional observation separately from anything you actually observe. List two possible explanations, such as how the holder rests or the direction of the pull; label them guesses.
Step 2: If you have a safe paper setup, repeat one removal and describe it without explaining the cause. Otherwise sketch the proposed observation and mark it unperformed.
Step 3: Change only one arrangement detail and repeat. A change that coincides with different movement does not settle the cause; record other uncontrolled details.
Step 4: Write one next check and one stopping condition. Stop after one comparison or when the setup cannot be tried safely; an unresolved cause is an acceptable completion.

Record and completion: Make columns for initial condition, observed action, possible explanation, single change, observed result and unresolved factors. Keep fictional and actual entries explicitly separated.
Reflection: Did you want to keep tracing the cause, or only finish fixing the object? Which uncertainty was interesting and which was frustrating? What condition would you change before another try?
Boundaries: Paper only: no dismantling devices, batteries, mains power, heat or moving mechanisms. This is not fault-finding certification or proof of technical ability.

content.title: Investigative
content.core_drive: Interest in asking questions, gathering evidence, and analyzing causes to understand why things work as they do. Reading research material, comparing explanations, and testing hypotheses are typical activities.
possible_drains: Research tasks often involve incomplete information, repeated checking, and accepting that conclusions remain uncertain. Different fields also require relevant knowledge and methodological training. Interest can be a starting point for learning.
context_costs: Research tasks often involve incomplete information, repeated checking, and accepting that conclusions remain uncertain. Different fields also require relevant knowledge and methodological training. Interest can be a starting point for learning.
misread_guardrails: Interest in research is distinct from intelligence, subject knowledge, and research skills. The score cannot demonstrate these abilities or determine a specific field of study.
validation_questions: Do I want to spend time checking evidence, modeling, and comparing evidence, or do I mainly want a quick answer?
What training, data access, or professional background does this question require?
When there is no clear answer, do I want to keep asking questions or move on to carrying something out?
content.positive_value: The appeal may lie in the question itself or in the process of checking evidence and reasoning. Notice whether you want to investigate inconsistencies, revise explanations, and keep exploring when there is no conclusion yet.
content.real_world_cost: Research tasks often involve incomplete information, repeated checking, and accepting that conclusions remain uncertain. Different fields also require relevant knowledge and methodological training. Interest can be a starting point for learning.
content.high_score_reading: In this response, you expressed greater interest in analysis and inquiry. You could first try looking up information, comparing evidence, or explaining a phenomenon, and observe which questions you want to explore in depth.
work_activity_examples: Turn a vague question into one that can be checked against evidence
Compare information from different sources
Propose different explanations for the same phenomenon
Design observations that distinguish between explanations
content.common_misread: Interest in research is distinct from intelligence, subject knowledge, and research skills. The score cannot demonstrate these abilities or determine a specific field of study.
content.action_advice: Choose a question you are curious about. Start with a question, evidence-checking, or hypothesis activity below, then look back at the step that most interested you.

boundaries.user_visible_boundary: The interpretations below describe interest in activities. Skills, qualifications, and career choices require other information as well.

content.title: Artistic
content.core_drive: Interest in creating, expressing ideas, and exploring different forms by turning ideas into writing, images, sound, or performance. These activities usually allow multiple forms of expression rather than one standard answer.
possible_drains: Creative work often involves revisions, feedback, deadlines, and audience requirements. Personal and commercial projects may offer different levels of freedom. Understanding these conditions can help you consider whether your interest will continue.
context_costs: Creative work often involves revisions, feedback, deadlines, and audience requirements. Personal and commercial projects may offer different levels of freedom. Understanding these conditions can help you consider whether your interest will continue.
misread_guardrails: The Artistic score reflects interest in creative activities. It does not evaluate the quality of your work, your creativity, or your aesthetic ability.
validation_questions: Which part do I most want to continue: developing ideas, choosing a style, refining versions, or adjusting after feedback?
What training, tools, aesthetic standards, or conditions for collaboration does this task require?
When the work is evaluated, does my interest grow, weaken, or shift to another part of the activity?
content.positive_value: The appeal may lie in developing a new angle, choosing a style, or repeatedly refining a piece of work. Distinguish whether you prefer creating freely, communicating to an audience, or improving existing content.
content.real_world_cost: Creative work often involves revisions, feedback, deadlines, and audience requirements. Personal and commercial projects may offer different levels of freedom. Understanding these conditions can help you consider whether your interest will continue.
content.high_score_reading: In this response, you expressed greater interest in creating and expressing ideas. You could first try different media, such as writing, visuals, or sound, and compare which forms you want to keep refining.
work_activity_examples: Develop different ways to express the same topic
Turn complex information into an explanatory diagram
Write, take photographs, or make a sound piece
Revise the structure and style of a piece of work in response to feedback
content.common_misread: The Artistic score reflects interest in creative activities. It does not evaluate the quality of your work, your creativity, or your aesthetic ability.
content.action_advice: Choose a form of expression below and finish a small piece of work. Then look back at whether you want to revise it and what you would change.

content.title: Realistic
content.core_drive: Interest in using tools, working with materials, or caring for tangible things through hands-on work with visible results. Repair, making things, operating equipment, and outdoor work can all involve these activities.
interest_activity_focus: Using tools and making physical objects
possible_drains: Physical demands, safety training, and coordination on site vary widely between settings. Enjoying model making does not necessarily mean enjoying long periods of outdoor work. Learning about specific tasks and conditions is more useful than looking only at job titles.
context_costs: Physical demands, safety training, and coordination on site vary widely between settings. Enjoying model making does not necessarily mean enjoying long periods of outdoor work. Learning about specific tasks and conditions is more useful than looking only at job titles.
misread_guardrails: Realistic interest does not mean strong practical skills, and it does not mean being limited to physical work. Actual skills and training conditions need separate consideration.
validation_questions: Which part do I most want to continue: working with tools and materials, troubleshooting on site, or turning steps into a visible result?
What training, safety requirements, or resources does this activity involve?
Does the interest remain when the setting or position of responsibility changes?
content.positive_value: The appeal of these activities often comes from working directly with something: adjusting a part, testing a material, or getting equipment running again. Notice whether you enjoy making things, troubleshooting, or seeing a tangible result.
content.real_world_cost: Physical demands, safety training, and coordination on site vary widely between settings. Enjoying model making does not necessarily mean enjoying long periods of outdoor work. Learning about specific tasks and conditions is more useful than looking only at job titles.
content.high_score_reading: In this response, you expressed greater interest in working hands-on with tangible things. You could first explore activities involving operating, making, or troubleshooting on site, then compare how different materials, tools, and work settings feel to you.
work_activity_examples: Assemble or repair a simple object
Make and adjust a physical model
Observe equipment in operation and record anything unusual
Compare how materials differ in practical use
content.common_misread: Realistic interest does not mean strong practical skills, and it does not mean being limited to physical work. Actual skills and training conditions need separate consideration.
content.action_advice: Choose something familiar from the activities below and try operating it or observing it. Afterwards, look back at the part you most wanted to continue.

content.title: Social
content.core_drive: Interest in helping people understand problems, learn, and grow through explaining, listening, guiding, or supporting. The focus is on the process of helping people, rather than simply how often you interact with them.
possible_drains: Supporting others requires communication, patience, and clear limits of responsibility. Some roles also involve professional qualifications and emotional demands. Everyday help and professional services have different requirements.
context_costs: Supporting others requires communication, patience, and clear limits of responsibility. Some roles also involve professional qualifications and emotional demands. Everyday help and professional services have different requirements.
misread_guardrails: Social interest does not mean being outgoing, kind, or well liked. An interest in helping others also cannot replace the professional training needed for teaching, counseling, or care.
validation_questions: Which part do I most want to continue: understanding needs, explaining information, offering companionship and support, or coordinating resources?
What ethical boundaries, professional training, or capacity to handle emotional demands does this interaction require?
Does my interest remain steady when responsibility increases or the person receiving support changes?
content.positive_value: The appeal may lie in understanding someone's needs, helping them learn something, or helping resolve a specific difficulty. Observe whether you prefer teaching, listening, or finding a way forward together.
content.real_world_cost: Supporting others requires communication, patience, and clear limits of responsibility. Some roles also involve professional qualifications and emotional demands. Everyday help and professional services have different requirements.
content.medium_score_reading: You may be willing to help others with familiar topics or within familiar relationships without wanting an ongoing support role. The person, communication style, and scope of responsibility may affect your willingness.
work_activity_examples: Explain a concept and respond to questions
Listen and check what the person actually needs
Help someone practice a skill you know
Organize materials suited to a particular learner
content.common_misread: Social interest does not mean being outgoing, kind, or well liked. An interest in helping others also cannot replace the professional training needed for teaching, counseling, or care.
content.action_advice: Choose a situation where you can offer everyday help within your abilities. With the other person's willingness to participate, look back at which kind of support you enjoyed.

content.title: Enterprising
content.core_drive: Interest in advancing goals, gaining support, coordinating resources, or influencing decisions. Starting projects, explaining proposals, negotiating, and organizing progress can all involve these activities.
possible_drains: Moving work forward often involves disagreement, pressure for results, and uncertainty. Decision-making authority, resources, and responsibility differ between roles. Enjoying starting projects does not mean wanting every management responsibility.
context_costs: Moving work forward often involves disagreement, pressure for results, and uncertainty. Decision-making authority, resources, and responsibility differ between roles. Enjoying starting projects does not mean wanting every management responsibility.
misread_guardrails: Enterprising interest does not mean you must start a business, and it does not demonstrate leadership or business judgment. It describes interest in influencing, organizing, and moving things forward.
validation_questions: Which part do I most want to continue: setting goals, securing resources, persuading people to collaborate, or making choices about risk?
What authority, resources, responsibility, and capacity to handle risk does this task require?
Am I still willing to keep moving it forward when the outcome is uncertain or feedback slows down?
content.positive_value: The appeal may lie in finding opportunities, persuading others, or moving something forward. Distinguish whether you prefer proposing a direction, securing resources, or coordinating implementation.
content.real_world_cost: Moving work forward often involves disagreement, pressure for results, and uncertainty. Decision-making authority, resources, and responsibility differ between roles. Enjoying starting projects does not mean wanting every management responsibility.
content.medium_score_reading: Your willingness to move things forward may depend on whether you support the goal and whether resources are available. Think back to where you wanted to take the initiative and where you preferred to help carry things out.
work_activity_examples: Explain a proposal to others and seek support
Compare the resources needed to reach a goal
Coordinate a group's responsibilities and progress
Discuss workable arrangements when views differ
content.common_misread: Enterprising interest does not mean you must start a business, and it does not demonstrate leadership or business judgment. It describes interest in influencing, organizing, and moving things forward.
content.action_advice: Choose a small shared task with clear responsibilities. Look back at whether you preferred initiating it, communicating, or organizing its execution.

content.title: Conventional
content.core_drive: Interest in organizing information, checking details, and maintaining processes under clear rules. Classifying, recording, checking data, and handling tasks in an orderly way are common activities.
possible_drains: Jobs differ in their demands for repetition, accuracy, and meeting deadlines. Enjoying organizing information does not necessarily mean enjoying long periods of repeated data entry. The clarity of a process and the reasonableness of its standards also affect the experience.
context_costs: Jobs differ in their demands for repetition, accuracy, and meeting deadlines. Enjoying organizing information does not necessarily mean enjoying long periods of repeated data entry. The clarity of a process and the reasonableness of its standards also affect the experience.
misread_guardrails: Conventional interest does not mean being conservative, lacking creativity, or being reliable at work. An interest score cannot replace an evaluation of attention to detail or actual work quality.
validation_questions: Which part do I most want to continue: organizing, checking, building a process, or keeping records consistent?
What understanding of rules, system access, or responsibility for errors does this task require?
Does my interest grow or decline when rules change or repetition increases?
content.positive_value: The appeal may lie in making information clear, finding errors, or keeping a process running steadily. Distinguish whether you prefer establishing order, following existing steps, or improving details.
content.real_world_cost: Jobs differ in their demands for repetition, accuracy, and meeting deadlines. Enjoying organizing information does not necessarily mean enjoying long periods of repeated data entry. The clarity of a process and the reasonableness of its standards also affect the experience.
content.low_score_safe_reading: In this response, activities with clear rules and substantial repetition held relatively limited appeal. This does not mean you are careless or unable to complete work according to standards.
work_activity_examples: Organize information and establish classification rules
Check the differences between two records
Write a procedure for a common task
Maintain a checklist and track the status of items
content.common_misread: Conventional interest does not mean being conservative, lacking creativity, or being reliable at work. An interest score cannot replace an evaluation of attention to detail or actual work quality.
content.action_advice: Choose a set of real information that contains nothing sensitive. Try organizing or checking it, then look back at whether you enjoyed the order, finding errors, or improving the process.

content.positive_value: The value of this content is to break the clues into observable small tasks: Investigative focuses on questions, evidence, mechanisms, variables, and ways of explaining; Artistic focuses on expression, style, narrative, form, and experience; Realistic focuses on tangible objects, tools, on-site conditions, materials, and visible results. Whichever comes first only indicates which activity to gather evidence from first. These clues offer exploration questions, not job answers.
content.real_world_cost: Reading boundary: these three clues may occur in different parts of one task or across different environments. Record only the appeal of specific activities, points of hesitation, and conditions you want to adjust. Do not turn the score order into a ranking of abilities or a fixed way of working.
content.activity_chain: Observe in order: first analyze questions, evidence, variables, or ways of explaining; then try different approaches to expression, style, narrative, or form; finally work with tangible objects, tools, or on-site conditions.
content.core_reading: These three leading interest dimensions indicate that Investigative, Artistic, Realistic activities stand relatively high in this response. IAR only sets a reading order: Investigative is the initial observation entry point, with Artistic and Realistic as additional entry points. It cannot establish a personality identity, ability level, or career conclusion.
content.first_experiment: Spend 30 minutes on a low-risk observation: first include an activity involving inquiry, then one involving expression, and finally one involving hands-on. Record only which part you most want to continue.
content.ordered_code_handling: IAR is the ordered three-letter code for this assessment: the first dimension, Investigative, is the initial observation entry point; the second, Artistic, and the third, Realistic, are additional entry points. The order changes what to ask first and what to explore next. It is not a fixed identity, an ability conclusion, or a career answer.
content.low_risk_validation: Low-risk observation: choose a small task that accommodates inquiry, expression, and hands-on clues. Record the three activities separately and look only at activity preferences and evidence of wanting to continue.
content.primary_activity_chain: Start with the first dimension, Investigative: use it as the initial observation entry point and look for small-task evidence involving questions, evidence, mechanisms, variables, and ways of explaining.
content.secondary_support_line: Then consider the second dimension, Artistic: use it as an additional observation entry point and record whether expression, style, narrative, form, and experience make the task more appealing.
content.tertiary_stabilizer: The third dimension, Realistic, is only an additional clue: observe whether tangible objects, tools, on-site conditions, materials, and visible results help distinguish more specific task conditions.
content.likely_tension: Differences between the three clues are worth exploring through small tasks. Observing one action and one condition at a time is more reliable than treating the three leading interests as a fixed way of working.

content.pair_tension: Tension in the combination often appears when a task rewards only one of the activities: hands-on clues may involve building, adjusting, repairing, or troubleshooting on site, while expression clues may involve drafting an expression, adjusting style, rewriting a narrative, or making versions in different forms. content.positive_value: The value of these clues is to observe the two activities separately and then together: first, work with tangible objects, tools, or on-site conditions; then, try different approaches to expression, style, narrative, or form. Finally, record whether they support each other or pull against each other within the same task.
content.real_world_cost: A reminder about practical conditions: if a task, environment, or role responsibility only accommodates hands-on or only expression, the other clue may be obscured. Training requirements, access to resources, the pace of feedback, and the extent of responsibility need separate checking.
content.common_misread: A common misreading is to treat hands-on and expression as a kind of person, a career direction, a set of abilities, or a person's actual responsibilities. faq_items.q: How do I read a three-letter code? For example, IAS?
faq_items.a: In the example IAS, I means Investigative, A means Artistic, and S means Social. Read the three letters shown in your own report as the interest dimensions that stand out in that result. Their order describes that result ranking, not a fixed identity.

faq_items.q: Does this tell me which career I should choose?
faq_items.a: No. It points to work activities that may be worth exploring or validating first. Real choices also depend on ability, experience, opportunity, values, entry barriers, and market conditions.

faq_items.q: Does a score of 80 mean I scored higher than 80% of people?
faq_items.a: No. The current 0-100 score is a within-form interest-strength conversion. It is not a population percentile and it is not an ability score.

faq_items.q: Does low E mean I cannot start a business, sell, or manage?
faq_items.a: No. Low E only means high-persuasion, high-exposure, and high-competition activities may not be the most natural interest entry point. Capability still depends on skills, experience, and real opportunities.

faq_items.q: Does low R mean I cannot do technical or hands-on work?
faq_items.a: No. Low R does not mean clumsy or unable to learn technical work. It means tools, field work, and physical operation may not be the most natural interest entry point right now.

faq_items.q: Is 140Q more accurate?
faq_items.a: Do not read it that way. 140Q observes tasks, environments, and role responsibilities in more context. It does not overturn 60Q and it does not compare raw scores across forms.

faq_items.q: What if I disagree with the result?
faq_items.a: Record the disagreement, check answer quality, near ties, and activity imagination, then use low-risk experiments or a same-form retest to validate. Feedback does not change scores.

faq_items.q: Why are occupation examples not expanded into a direct list?
faq_items.a: Occupation names are easy to misread as conclusions. FermatMind shows activities and tasks first. Occupation names are only context examples and must keep source status visible.

faq_items.q: Can I share the report with a teacher, counselor, or friend?
faq_items.a: Start with the safe share version. When a full report includes personal interest structure or feedback history, you should decide whether to show it.

faq_items.q: Can an employer use this for screening?
faq_items.a: No. This report must not be used for recruiting, admission, promotion, elimination, or qualification decisions.

faq_items.q: Why does the result page include Action Lab?
faq_items.a: Career interests need real-world validation. Action Lab supports low-risk experiments and does not generate career conclusions.

faq_items.q: What if a retest looks different?
faq_items.a: First check whether it used the same form, answer quality, near ties, and your state at the time. Do not chart raw score gains or drops across different forms.

faq_items.q: Can a Holland Code change over time?
faq_items.a: Interest structure often has some stability, but experience, opportunity, and environment can affect expression. Treat retesting as a clue about change, not a win-or-lose result.

faq_items.q: How is this different from an ability test?
faq_items.a: RIASEC looks at interest in activities. It does not decide whether you are already good at them. Ability needs other evidence.

faq_items.q: Why not just tell me the single path I should take?
faq_items.a: A direct conclusion can hide real-world constraints. A steadier approach is to read activities, tasks, environments, and roles first, then test small next steps.

faq_items.q: If I already have a target occupation, should I still read RIASEC?
faq_items.a: Yes. Put the target into aspiration calibration and read which activities overlap with current interest clues, and which real-world parts still need validation.

faq_items.q: Can I show the PDF to a counselor?
faq_items.a: Yes, but once a PDF is forwarded the platform cannot remotely recall it. A counselor discussion version should be used only with your permission.

faq_items.q: Why does the result page not show every score detail by default?
faq_items.a: The default view shows levels and explanations to reduce false precision. Expanded views can show more evidence when appropriate.

faq_items.q: Is a higher score always better?
faq_items.a: No. High interest can be a more natural energy entry point, but it can also carry practical costs. Low interest is not a defect.

faq_items.q: Can I use this report to choose a college major?
faq_items.a: It can be an exploration input, but not the only basis. Major decisions also depend on course content, ability foundation, portfolio, resources, location, and long-term commitment.

task_examples: Materials and fictional brief: Fictional note: “The desk is always confusing. A slip was hard to find on Monday, four slips were found quickly on Tuesday, and nobody recorded where the slips were placed.” The days and events are invented. Use this note and a blank sheet.

Scope and conditions: Use only your own non-sensitive materials or the supplied fiction. No paid tool, account, outside contact or public posting is required. A willing partner already present is optional except where live interaction is explicitly needed; solo preparation never counts as another person’s feedback. Stop or pause at any point. Timing is a flexible planning aid, not a performance limit.
Step 1: Underline observations, evaluative words and missing information using three labels rather than relying on colour. Do not upgrade “always confusing” into a measured fact.

Step 2: Write a narrower question that names an action and a condition: for example, what happens when the slips have one labelled place? List what “hard to find” would need to mean in an observation.
Step 3: Draw a small observation plan with the same item set and one layout change. State what you would record and what this small plan would not establish.
Step 4: Rewrite the question once after finding a missing condition. Keep both versions and one alternative question rather than forcing a single correct formulation.
Record and completion: Keep a known/unknown/assumption list, two versions of the question and a proposed observation. No experiment or fictional observation becomes a measured personal result.

Reflection: Which part made you curious: defining words, isolating a condition or designing an observation? Would you want to investigate the revised question? Note if the topic itself was uninteresting.
Boundaries: No new user study, timings, participant claims or data collection is required. A question plan is the output; do not invent results to finish it.

Optional continuation: Optional: take one additional short round of this same exercise, changing one condition named in your reflection. Keep the two records; do not treat ease or improvement as an interest score. Optional, up to two hours only if useful: develop this same small output with materials already available. Use only fictional or your own non-sensitive material; no outside contact or spending. Stop after a documented revision rather than filling the time. Optional: repeat this same exercise twice on dates you choose, changing one condition and noting engagement and effort. These observations do not establish a lasting interest or validate a test.

task_examples: Materials and fictional brief: Three invented source cards concern a paper holder. Card A, an observation note: “With ten cards, the base moved during one removal; pull direction not recorded.” Card B, a material note: “This model used thin paper; no comparison with thick card.” Card C, a comment: “I like the appearance; I did not try removing a card.” None is an external research source.

Scope and conditions: Use only your own non-sensitive materials or the supplied fiction. No paid tool, account, outside contact or public posting is required. A willing partner already present is optional except where live interaction is explicitly needed; solo preparation never counts as another person’s feedback. Stop or pause at any point. Timing is a flexible planning aid, not a performance limit.
Step 1: Write a question: what do these notes tell us about using the holder? Keep the three source labels and their exact stated limitations.
Step 2: For each card, record the claim it supports and one claim it cannot support. Appearance approval cannot establish ease of removal; a single movement cannot explain its cause.
Step 3: Place one apparent disagreement side by side. Decide whether it is a real contradiction or concerns different aspects. Mark missing corroboration instead of counting notes as votes.
Step 4: Write a cautious two-sentence account and the next evidence you would want. Do not search for people, buy materials or claim that the invented cards establish real product facts.
Record and completion: Produce a three-row evidence table: source card, observation or opinion, supported statement, limit and next evidence. Retain “unknown” when no card answers the question.
Reflection: Did comparing scope and uncertainty make you want to examine another source? Did you prefer resolving the question quickly? Keep that response separate from the quality of your summary.
Boundaries: All three cards are fictional teaching material. They are not three genuine independent sources, peer-reviewed findings or evidence of an occupation.
